\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursively training language models on their own outputs erodes distributional tails, eventually collapsing the output distribution to a narrow mode.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this phenomenon through scaling laws that distinguish tail \emph{narrowing} (reduced variance) from tail \emph{cutting} (lost support), showing both accelerate with recursion depth.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this analysis to self-consuming generative models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff as synthetic data accumulates across generations.
\citet{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} show that retaining real data alongside synthetic data across generations mitigates collapse, while \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} demonstrate that filtering synthetic samples via binary detection can preserve model quality.
Recent work further refines the theoretical picture: \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} identify non-monotonic dynamics where early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality before eventual degradation; \citet{marchi2024_heat_death} characterize convergence to a fixed-point ``heat death'' distribution; and \citet{wang2026_contamination} derive contamination guarantees bounding how much synthetic data a corpus can absorb.
Additional lines of work address curated synthetic pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse in factual recall \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures of model-generated text \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and the ``synthetic eggs'' problem in self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation patterns but assume the generation depth is known a priori; our work addresses the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature---the tendency of model-generated text to occupy local maxima of the log-probability surface---as a zero-shot detection signal.
\citet{fast_detectgpt2024} improve computational efficiency by replacing random perturbations with conditional probability curvature from a surrogate model.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits the perplexity ratio between two related models, achieving strong detection without training data.
DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity patterns, while GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} provides statistical visualization of per-token likelihood ranks for human inspection.
\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} expose fundamental limits: paraphrasing attacks reduce detection accuracy to near chance, and \citet{pudasaini2026_detection_fails} show detection degrades under distribution shift between training and deployment domains.
\citet{pu2026_generator_barrier} formalize a generator barrier bounding detection performance when the generator is unknown.
All these methods perform binary classification (human vs.\ machine), discarding the ordinal depth information that distinguishes first-generation from deeply recursive text.
Our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the \emph{extent} of editing applied to a passage---a continuous measure of how much a text has been modified in a single pass---but does not model recursive generation chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} formulate authorship attribution as multi-source classification, identifying \emph{which} model generated a text rather than \emph{how many} recursive steps it has undergone.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} provides a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple synthetic data modalities but evaluates binary detection, not depth estimation.
These tasks probe complementary dimensions of synthetic text characterization; none estimates recursive depth.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
The choice of decoding strategy shapes the statistical properties of generated text in ways that interact with recursive depth signals.
\citet{holtzman2020_nucleus} show that unrestricted sampling produces degenerate repetitions and propose nucleus sampling to maintain output diversity.
\citet{finlayson2024_closing} demonstrate that decoding parameters affect downstream evaluation metrics in non-trivial ways.
\citet{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded} find that the effect of decoding strategies on text quality is model-dependent, complicating universal quality claims.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} provide a systematic comparison of decoding methods on surface-level text properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} introduces perplexity-controlled decoding that actively regulates output entropy.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects that go beyond single-pass text quality to shape the discriminability of recursive depth itself.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all generation depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking schemes \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} require proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively to existing corpora.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterizes how recursive training degrades model quality but assumes the generation depth is known a priori---the very quantity we seek to estimate.
\citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} show that filtering synthetic data from training corpora can prevent collapse, yet their approach relies on binary detection and does not distinguish among recursive depths.
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the extent of single-pass editing applied to a text but does not address multi-step recursive generation.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints exhibit universal stability across model families and decoding strategies.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by Gini importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, distinguishing it from binary detection and single-pass editing estimation. We introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells (100\%) and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 7/9 (78\%), with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. The extended Pythia nucleus pipeline (d0--d5) yields $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$, establishing that depth discrimination persists through four recursive steps before falling below threshold.

    \item \textbf{Generalization analysis.} Cross-model leave-one-out transfer achieves 66.4\% mean accuracy and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\% (chance = 25\%), demonstrating partial universality of depth fingerprints. We identify a temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion (GPT-2~XL: 0.13, OLMo: 0.25) caused by accelerated convergence. Z-score normalization recovers logistic regression performance for non-temperature holdouts (d1v2 AUC 0.61--0.89) but fails to resolve the temperature-specific inversion, revealing a two-layer covariate shift structure.

    \item \textbf{End-to-end learning as negative result.} Deep Contrastive Ordinal Learning (DCOL) with RoBERTa-large, tested across 6 configurations, achieves at best 64.5\% versus 78.2\% for RF on the same data, with 5 of 6 runs failing due to embedding collapse, OOM, or NaN losses. This suggests that explicit statistical features capture depth-relevant information that end-to-end models struggle to extract from raw text.
\end{itemize}

1	\section{Generalization and Robustness}
2	\label{sec:generalization}
3	
4	The atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) established in-distribution accuracy of 69.6--85.4\%.
5	We now test whether these results reflect genuine statistical regularities or artifacts of specific training conditions, evaluating four axes: classifier choice (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}), cross-model transfer (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossmodel}), cross-strategy transfer (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}), and end-to-end learned representations (\S\ref{sec:gen:dcol}).
6	
7	\subsection{Baseline Comparison}
8	\label{sec:gen:baselines}
9	
10	Table~\ref{tab:baselines} compares classification methods on the Pythia-1.4B nucleus setting.
11	Three feature-based methods---Random Forest (RF), CORAL ordinal regression \cite{coral2020}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026}---all operate on the same 19 statistical features and achieve near-identical accuracy (78.1--78.2\%).
12	A cross-entropy MLP and logistic regression trail by $\sim$3 percentage points.
13	Single-feature regression on mean perplexity performs at chance (25.1\%), confirming that depth estimation requires the multi-dimensional feature representation defined in \S\ref{sec:method}.
14

16	\centering
17	\small
18	\caption{Comparison of classification methods on Pythia-1.4B nucleus. RF, CORAL, and DivEye use the same 19 statistical features. Chance = 25\%.}
19	\label{tab:baselines}

21	\toprule
22	Method & 4-class Acc (\%) \\
23	\midrule
24	RF (19 features) & \textbf{78.2} \\
25	CORAL & 78.1 \\
26	DivEye & 78.2 \\
27	CE-MLP & 74.9 \\

34	\end{table}
35	
36	RF and CORAL achieve near-identical accuracy (gap $<$0.5pp), both outperforming DivEye and LR, indicating that the discriminative signal resides in the features rather than the classifier.
37	A zero-shot LLM baseline (DeepSeek V3.2) achieves 40.0\%---above chance but 38 points below feature-based methods.

49

54	\centering
55	\small

57	\label{tab:cross_model}

78

83	\centering

85	\caption{Cross-strategy transfer (leave-one-out). Train on 2 strategies, test on held-out 3rd. Chance = 25\%.}

100	
101	\paragraph{Temperature-induced boundary inversion.}
102	Training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1v2 AUC of 0.129 for GPT-2~XL and 0.253 for OLMo---both below 0.5, indicating that the d1/d2 decision boundary \emph{inverts} (Pythia retains a degraded 0.576).
103	This follows from the trajectory analysis in \S\ref{sec:atlas}: temperature sampling shifts feature values at depth $d$ toward depth $d{+}1$ under nucleus/top-$k$.
104	
105	\paragraph{Z-score normalization does not resolve the inversion.}
106	A natural hypothesis is that per-feature z-score normalization might correct this covariate shift \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting}.
107	For RF, z-normalization leaves accuracy essentially unchanged (59.1\% $\to$ 59.2\%) and does not improve d1v2 AUC ($\Delta < 0.02$), as expected since tree splits depend on feature rank order, not scale.
108	Z-score standardization substantially improves logistic regression cross-strategy transfer for nucleus and top-$k$ holdouts (d1v2 AUC 0.61--0.89), but fails to resolve the temperature-induced inversion (d1v2 AUC remains near or below chance: Pythia 0.52, GPT-2~XL 0.24, OLMo 0.19).
109	This two-layer structure---scale shift addressable by normalization, plus a deeper geometric shift specific to temperature sampling---suggests that temperature decoding induces qualitatively different feature distributions that cannot be reconciled by linear rescaling.
110	
111	\subsection{End-to-End Learning: A Negative Result}
112	\label{sec:gen:dcol}
113	
114	We test whether end-to-end learning can bypass feature engineering via Deep Contrastive Ordinal Learning (DCOL) with a RoBERTa-large encoder.
115	Across six configurations, DCOL fails to match feature-based methods: five runs suffer training instabilities (embedding collapse, OOM, gradient explosion), and the best run (v6) reaches only 64.5\% (vs.\ RF 78.2\%) with severe overfitting (train 75\% vs.\ val 64.4\% at epoch 1).
116	This suggests that explicit statistical features capture depth-relevant tail behavior that end-to-end models struggle to extract from raw text.

1	\section{The Depth Degradation Atlas}
2	\label{sec:atlas}
3	
4	We systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes the statistical profile of text across a grid of 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 generation depths (d0--d3), yielding 9 experimental configurations each spanning 4 depths.
5	For each cell we train a Random Forest (RF) classifier on the 19 statistical features defined in \S\ref{sec:method} and examine (i)~in-distribution depth classification accuracy, (ii)~which features carry depth signal, (iii)~how far into the recursion chain depth remains discriminable, and (iv)~how decoding strategy modulates the degradation trajectory.
6	
7	\subsection{In-Distribution Performance}
8	\label{sec:atlas:indist}
9	
10	Table~\ref{tab:main_matrix} reports 4-class depth estimation accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation.
11	All 9 cells exceed chance (25\%) by a wide margin, with accuracy ranging from 69.6\% to 85.4\%.
12	Both model family and decoding strategy influence accuracy, with consistent model ordering (GPT-2~XL $>$ OLMo $>$ Pythia) and strategy ordering (temp $\geq$ nucleus $>$ top-$k$) across all settings.
13	Among strategies, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$) yields the best accuracy in 2 of 3 model families, while top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) trails by 6--9 percentage points.
14	
15	\begin{table}[t]
16	\centering
17	\small
18	\caption{In-distribution 4-class depth estimation accuracy (\%) across 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies. RF classifier with 19 statistical features, 5-fold CV. Chance = 25\%.}
19	\label{tab:main_matrix}
20	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
21	\toprule
22	Model & Nucleus & Temp & Top-$k$ \\
23	 & $p{=}0.95$ & $\tau{=}0.9$ & $k{=}50$ \\
24	\midrule
25	Pythia-1.4B & 78.2 & 76.3 & 69.6 \\
26	OLMo-1B & 78.8 & 82.0 & 74.2 \\
27	GPT-2 XL & 83.3 & \textbf{85.4} & 76.6 \\
28	\bottomrule
29	\end{tabular}
30	\end{table}
31	
32	Because the human-written seed text (d0) is often trivially separable from any machine-generated depth, we also evaluate 3-class accuracy excluding d0.
33	Performance drops moderately---GPT-2~XL with temperature sampling still reaches 82.0\%, and even the weakest setting (Pythia nucleus) retains 70.8\%---confirming that the classifier captures inter-generation differences beyond the human--machine boundary.
34	
35	\subsection{Feature Universality}
36	\label{sec:atlas:features}
37	
38	To identify which statistical fingerprints carry depth signal, we train a dedicated binary RF per cell (d$_i$ vs.\ rest) and extract Gini importances.
39	Figure~\ref{fig:atlas_heatmap} visualizes the top-7 feature importances across all 9 cells.
40	
41	Two features dominate.
42	The 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells, while surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surp}) does so in 7 of 9.
43	In the two exceptions---GPT-2~XL with temperature and top-$k$ sampling---the 75th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p75\_ppl}) replaces surprisal variance in the top 2, though surprisal variance remains among the top 4 features.
44	To quantify cross-model agreement, we compute the Spearman rank correlation of the full 19-feature importance vectors across all $\binom{9}{2}=36$ cell pairs and obtain a mean $\rho = 0.868$ (range: 0.619--0.954).
45	
46	\begin{figure}[t]
47	\centering
48	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../../figures/paper/fig_atlas_heatmap.pdf}
49	\caption{Feature importance heatmap across 9 cells (3 models $\times$ 3 strategies). Top-7 features by mean Gini importance. \textsc{p90\_ppl} appears in the top 2 for all cells; \textsc{var\_surp} for 7 of 9.}
50	\label{fig:atlas_heatmap}
51	\end{figure}
52	
53	These results align with theoretical predictions: recursive finetuning erodes the tail of the token-probability distribution \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}, and high-percentile perplexity directly measures tail behavior.
54	The universality of these markers across architectures and decoding strategies suggests they reflect a structural property of the recursive generation process rather than model-specific artifacts.
55	
56	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
57	\label{sec:atlas:edd}
58	
59	Aggregate accuracy masks the fact that adjacent depths become harder to distinguish as depth increases.
60	We formalize this via the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD; defined in \S\ref{sec:method}): $\mathrm{EDD}_T$ is the maximum depth $d^*$ such that the pairwise AUC between $d^*$ and $d^*{+}1$ exceeds a threshold $T$, using a dedicated binary RF per adjacent pair.
61	
62	Within the 4-class atlas (d0--d3), 7 of 9 cells achieve $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=3$; the two exceptions are Pythia and OLMo with top-$k$ sampling ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=2$), consistent with top-$k$'s signal-attenuating effect noted in \S\ref{sec:atlas:indist}.
63	
64	To probe deeper, we extend the Pythia-1.4B nucleus pipeline to 6 depths (d0--d5) and train a 500-tree binary RF for each adjacent pair (we increase from 200 to 500 trees for binary classifiers to ensure convergence on the smaller per-pair sample sizes).
65	Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} shows the pairwise AUC decay curve.
66	The d0\,vs.\,d1 boundary is near-perfect (AUC\,=\,0.998), reflecting the well-known human--machine gap.
67	Subsequent boundaries degrade monotonically: d1\,vs.\,d2 achieves 0.925 [95\% CI: 0.914,\,0.935], d2\,vs.\,d3 reaches 0.823 [0.805,\,0.840], and d3\,vs.\,d4 yields 0.784 [0.765,\,0.802]---with the confidence interval lower bound still exceeding $T{=}0.75$.
68	At d4\,vs.\,d5, AUC drops to 0.683 [0.661,\,0.705], falling below the threshold and fixing $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=4$.
69	
70	\begin{figure}[t]
71	\centering
72	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../../figures/paper/fig_auc_decay.pdf}
73	\caption{Binary pairwise AUC between adjacent depths (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus $p{=}0.95$, d0--d5). Shaded bands: 95\% bootstrap CI. Dashed line: $T{=}0.75$. $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=4$: depth pairs up to d3\,vs.\,d4 remain discriminable.}
74	\label{fig:auc_decay}
75	\end{figure}
76	
77	Table~\ref{tab:edd_sensitivity} shows the sensitivity of EDD to the choice of threshold.
78	At $T{=}0.65$, all pairs through d4\,vs.\,d5 pass, giving $\mathrm{EDD}=5$.
79	At $T{=}0.80$, only d1\,vs.\,d2 and d2\,vs.\,d3 pass, yielding $\mathrm{EDD}=3$.
80	The d0\,vs.\,d1 pair passes at every threshold ($\text{AUC}\geq0.99$).
81	
82	\begin{table}[t]
83	\centering
84	\small
85	\caption{EDD sensitivity to threshold $T$ (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus $p{=}0.95$). \checkmark: pairwise AUC $\geq T$; ---: below $T$. d0\,vs.\,d1 always passes (AUC$\geq$0.99) and is omitted.}
86	\label{tab:edd_sensitivity}
87	\begin{tabular}{cccccr}
88	\toprule
89	$T$ & d1/d2 & d2/d3 & d3/d4 & d4/d5 & EDD \\
90	\midrule
91	0.65 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & 5 \\
92	0.70 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & --- & 4 \\
93	0.75 & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & --- & 4 \\
94	0.80 & \checkmark & \checkmark & --- & --- & 3 \\
95	\bottomrule
96	\end{tabular}
97	\end{table}
98	
99	\paragraph{Granularity ablation.}
100	Decision boundary dilution motivates EDD's binary-pair design: mean accuracy drops from 99.5\% (binary) to 78.3\% (4-class) to 62.9\% (6-class), and the d2\,vs.\,d3 AUC falls from 0.804 to 0.689 between the 4-class and 6-class settings for Pythia nucleus---a 14\% relative decline attributable to boundary dilution, not signal loss.
101	
102	\subsection{Strategy-Dependent Trajectories}
103	\label{sec:atlas:trajectories}
104	
105	The atlas reveals that decoding strategy does not merely scale the overall signal strength---it reshapes the degradation trajectory.
106	Figure~\ref{fig:feature_trajectory} plots normalized feature means across depths for three key features.
107	
108	\begin{figure}[t]
109	\centering

1	\section{The Depth Degradation Atlas}
2	\label{sec:atlas}
3	
4	We systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes the statistical profile of text across a grid of 3 model families $\times$ 3 decoding strategies $\times$ 4 generation depths (d0--d3), yielding 9 experimental configurations each spanning 4 depths.
5	For each cell we train a Random Forest (RF) classifier on the 19 statistical features defined in \S\ref{sec:method} and examine (i)~in-distribution depth classification accuracy, (ii)~which features carry depth signal, (iii)~how far into the recursion chain depth remains discriminable, and (iv)~how decoding strategy modulates the degradation trajectory.
6	
7	\subsection{In-Distribution Performance}
8	\label{sec:atlas:indist}
9	
10	Table~\ref{tab:main_matrix} reports 4-class depth estimation accuracy under 5-fold cross-validation.
11	All 9 cells exceed chance (25\%) by a wide margin, with accuracy ranging from 69.6\% to 85.4\%.
12	Both model family and decoding strategy influence accuracy, with model ordering GPT-2~XL $>$ OLMo $>$ Pythia holding across all strategies.
13	Top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) trails by 6--9 percentage points, while temperature and nucleus sampling alternate for the lead depending on model family.
14	
15	\begin{table}[t]

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "# Binary pairwise RF evaluation for d3v4 and d4v5.
# Dedicated binary classifiers to replace 6-class pairwise AUC
# (which suffers from decision boundary dilution).
# Also runs d1v2 and d2v3 as sanity checks (should match 4-class pipeline).

import json, sys
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path("/root/autodl-tmp/recursive_gen_depth_est")

FEATURE_COLS = [
    "mean_ppl", "var_ppl", "skewness_ppl", "kurtosis_ppl",
    "p10_ppl", "p25_ppl", "p50_ppl", "p75_ppl", "p90_ppl",
    "mean_surprisal", "var_surprisal", "entropy_of_surprisal",
    "type_token_ratio", "hapax_ratio",
    "bigram_entropy", "trigram_entropy",
    "rep_2gram", "rep_3gram", "rep_4gram",
]


def load_features(path):
    X, y = [], []
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            rec = json.loads(line)
            feats = [rec[c] for c in FEATURE_COLS]
            if not any(np.isnan(feats) | np.isinf(feats)):
                X.append(feats)
                y.append(rec["depth"])
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)


def find_and_load_all_features():
    """Search for features files covering depths 0-5."""
    candidates = [
        BASE / "results" / "depth_extension" / "features_all.jsonl",
        BASE / "results" / "depth_extension" / "features_6class.jsonl",
        BASE / "data" / "features_all_6class.jsonl",
    ]
    for c in candidates:
        if c.exists():
            print(f"Found combined features: {c}")
            return load_features(c)

    # Fallback: combine original d0-d3 + extension d4-d5
    print("No combined file found, assembling from individual sources...")
    X_all, y_all = [], []

    # d0-d3 from original pipeline
    orig = BASE / "data" / "features_all.jsonl"
    if orig.exists():
        X, y = load_features(orig)
        print(f"  Original features_all.jsonl: {len(X)} samples, depths {np.unique(y)}")
        X_all.append(X)
        y_all.append(y)

    # d4, d5 from depth extension
    for d in [4, 5]:
        for pattern in [
            BASE / "results" / "depth_extension" / f"features_depth_{d}.jsonl",
            BASE / "results" / "depth_extension" / f"depth_{d}_features.jsonl",
            BASE / "data" / f"features_depth_{d}.jsonl",
            BASE / "data" / f"depth_{d}_features.jsonl",
        ]:
            if pattern.exists():
                X, y = load_features(pattern)
                print(f"  Depth {d}: {len(X)} samples from {pattern}")
                X_all.append(X)
                y_all.append(y)
                break
        else:
            print(f"  WARNING: No features found for depth {d}")

    if not X_all:
        return np.array([]), np.array([])
    return np.vstack(X_all), np.concatenate(y_all)


def binary_rf_eval(X, y, d_low, d_high, seed=42, n_bootstrap=1000):
    mask = np.isin(y, [d_low, d_high])
    Xb = X[mask]
    yb = (y[mask] == d_high).astype(int)

    print(f"\n{'='*50}")
    print(f"Binary d{d_low}v{d_high}: {len(yb)} samples "
          f"(class0={np.sum(yb==0)}, class1={np.sum(yb==1)})")

    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        Xb, yb, test_size=0.2, stratify=yb, random_state=seed
    )
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=seed, n_jobs=-1)
    rf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

    y_prob = rf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    y_pred = rf.predict(X_te)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_te, y_prob)
    acc = accuracy_score(y_te, y_pred)
    prec = precision_score(y_te, y_pred)
    rec = recall_score(y_te, y_pred)

    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    aucs = []
    for _ in range(n_bootstrap):
        idx = rng.choice(len(y_te), len(y_te), replace=True)
        if len(np.unique(y_te[idx])) == 2:
            aucs.append(roc_auc_score(y_te[idx], y_prob[idx]))
    ci_lo, ci_hi = np.percentile(aucs, [2.5, 97.5])

    fi = rf.feature_importances_
    top5_idx = np.argsort(fi)[::-1][:5]
    top5 = [(FEATURE_COLS[i], round(float(fi[i]), 4)) for i in top5_idx]

    result = {
        "pair": f"d{d_low}v{d_high}",
        "auc": round(float(auc), 4),
        "auc_ci95": [round(float(ci_lo), 4), round(float(ci_hi), 4)],
        "accuracy": round(float(acc), 4),
        "precision": round(float(prec), 4),
        "recall": round(float(rec), 4),
        "n_train": int(len(y_tr)),
        "n_test": int(len(y_te)),
        "top5_features": top5,
    }

    print(f"  AUC:  {auc:.4f} [{ci_lo:.4f}, {ci_hi:.4f}]")
    print(f"  Acc:  {acc:.4f}  Prec: {prec:.4f}  Rec: {rec:.4f}")
    print(f"  Top5: {top5}")
    return result


def parse_args():
    import argparse
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Binary pairwise RF evaluation for depth extension")
    p.add_argument("--features_path", default=None, help="Path to combined features JSONL (skips auto-search)")
    p.add_argument("--output_dir", default=None, help="Output directory (default: results/binary_pairwise/)")
    return p.parse_args()


def main():
    args = parse_args()

    if args.features_path:
        print(f"Loading features from: {args.features_path}")
        X, y = load_features(args.features_path)
    else:
        X, y = find_and_load_all_features()
    if len(X) == 0:
        print("ERROR: No features loaded.")
        print("Listing potential directories:")
        for d in ["results/depth_extension", "data", "results"]:
            p = BASE / d
            if p.exists():
                files = list(p.glob("*.jsonl"))
                print(f"  {p}: {[f.name for f in files]}")
        sys.exit(1)

    depths_found = dict(zip(*np.unique(y, return_counts=True)))
    print(f"\nTotal: {len(X)} samples, depths: {depths_found}")

    # Run binary RF for d1v2, d2v3 (sanity check) + d3v4, d4v5 (target)
    results = {}
    for d_low, d_high in [(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5)]:
        if d_low in depths_found and d_high in depths_found:
            results[f"d{d_low}v{d_high}"] = binary_rf_eval(X, y, d_low, d_high)
        else:
            print(f"\nWARNING: Skipping d{d_low}v{d_high} — depth not in data")

    # EDD determination
    d3v4_auc = results.get("d3v4", {}).get("auc", 0)
    d4v5_auc = results.get("d4v5", {}).get("auc", 0)
    if d3v4_auc > 0.75 and d4v5_auc > 0.75:
        edd = ">=5"
    elif d3v4_auc > 0.75:
        edd = "4"
    else:
        edd = "3"

    print(f"\n{'='*50}")
    print(f"EDD DETERMINATION: d3v4={d3v4_auc:.4f}, d4v5={d4v5_auc:.4f} → EDD {edd}")

    # Reference: 4-class pipeline pairwise AUC (Pythia nucleus)
    ref = {"d0v1": 0.9975, "d1v2": 0.8607, "d2v3": 0.8005}
    print(f"\nSanity check vs 4-class pipeline:")
    for pair in ["d1v2", "d2v3"]:
        if pair in results:
            delta = results[pair]["auc"] - ref[pair]
            print(f"  {pair}: binary={results[pair]['auc']:.4f} vs 4-class={ref[pair]:.4f} (Δ={delta:+.4f})")

    # Save
    out_dir = Path(args.output_dir) if args.output_dir else BASE / "results" / "binary_pairwise"
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    output = {
        "pairs": results,
        "edd_determination": edd,
        "threshold": 0.75,
        "reference_4class": ref,
    }
    out_path = out_dir / "binary_pairwise_results.json"
    with open(out_path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(output, f, indent=2)
    print(f"\nResults saved to {out_path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
